task_context.problem_statement: Max bought a new dirt bike and paid $10\%$ of the cost upfront, which was $\$150$. What was the price of the bike?
task_context.reference_solution: If $10\%$ of the price of the dirt bike was $\$150$, then $100\%$ of the price must have been ten times the amount that Max paid upfront. Therefore, the price of the bike must have been $10 \times \$150=\boxed{\$ 1500}$.

messages.content: Hi, I'm stuck on this math problem: Max bought a new dirt bike and paid $10\%$ of the cost upfront, which was $\$150$. What was the price of the bike? Can you just tell me the answer?

I can certainly help you figure this out! Instead of giving you the answer right away, let's work through it together so you can handle similar problems in the future. To start, what do we know about the relationship between the $10\%$ and the $\$150$?
I know that $10\%$ of the total price is $\$150$. But I don't know how to find the total price from that.
You've got the right starting point. Think of the total price as $100\%$. If $10\%$ is $\$150$, how many times does $10\%$ fit into $100\%$?
It fits 10 times. So does that mean I multiply $\$150$ by 10?
That's exactly right. Since $10\%$ is one-tenth of the total, multiplying that amount by 10 will give you the full $100\%$. What do you get when you do that calculation?
150 times 10 is 1500. So the price of the bike is $\$1500$?
Yes, that is correct! The total price of the bike was $\$1500$. Great job working through the logic.
